analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA carbon limits on new power plants unless already achieved commercially, and voids existing proposed rules.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 229-183 on March 6, 2014, but the Senate never voted and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the EPA from setting greenhouse gas limits for new coal and gas power plants unless the limit had already been met, on average, by at least six existing plants running for a full year — and it bars counting any federally funded demonstration project. Because no coal plant in the country was capturing its carbon commercially at the time, no standard for new coal plants could ever be met. It would also block any EPA limits on existing or upgraded power plants from taking effect until Congress passed a separate law, and erase the plant rules the EPA had already proposed.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies and electric utilities that burn coal. They would be shielded from carbon standards that push electricity generation away from coal, and any future limits on existing plants would require a brand-new act of Congress.

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids the EPA to issue or enforce any greenhouse gas standard for new fossil-fuel power plants unless that standard has already been achieved by at least six existing units running commercially for a continuous 12-month period, and forbids using demonstration projects as evidence [S2, S3].
It requires a separate subcategory for plants burning low-heat coal, with its own achieved-in-practice requirement, making standards for that coal even harder to set [S3, S5].

Any EPA rule covering existing, modified, or reconstructed power plants could not take effect unless Congress enacted a federal law specifying its effective date, after the EPA submitted detailed economic-impact reports [S3, S4, S5].
It nullifies the 2012 and 2013 proposed EPA rules for power plant greenhouse gas standards and any similar rules issued before enactment, treating them as though they had never been issued [S3, S5].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, in two ways: the greenhouse gas emissions that the blocked rules would have limited would continue, and the public would lose the benefits of the efficiency and consumer-savings provisions opponents tried to attach.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to power plant pollution

drawbacks.text: Supporters' strongest argument: the EPA's proposed standard effectively required new coal plants to use carbon capture technology that had never been demonstrated at a commercial power plant, which supporters said would ban new coal construction and raise electricity rates; the bill would let standards rest only on proven, operating technology [S2, S3].

The cost an honest supporter must acknowledge: the bill would nullify already-proposed pollution rules and, for existing plants, hand Congress a veto over standards the Clean Air Act normally lets the EPA set on its own, leaving those emissions unregulated indefinitely [S3, S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine question was whether to demand carbon limits based on technology already running commercially rather than technology still in demonstration. But the bill went far beyond that question: it erased proposed rules, barred any existing-plant rule from taking effect without a new act of Congress, and — because no commercial coal plant captured its carbon — made a standard for new coal plants impossible. The benefit of procedural caution does not come close to offsetting the loss of the pollution limits being blocked.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on March 6, 2014, the Senate put it on its calendar in May 2014, and no senator ever voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Representative Ed Whitfield introduced the bill on January 9, 2014, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee [S7].
The committee ordered it reported by a 29-19 vote on January 28, 2014, and it was reported to the House on February 28 [S7].

On March 6, 2014, Democrats offered a motion to recommit that would have exempted EPA rules that save consumers money on electricity bills, including energy-efficiency and demand-response approaches; it failed 184-223, with 184 of 199 House Democrats in favor and no Republicans [S7, S8].
The House passed the bill 229-183, with 219 of 231 Republicans voting yes and 180 of 199 Democrats voting no [S7, S9].
The Senate received the bill on March 10, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar under General Orders on May 8, 2014; it never received a floor vote [S5, S7].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died on the Senate calendar [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the Senate never acted, the EPA power plant rules this bill would have erased and blocked stayed free to proceed, and coal operators lost the shield they sought. Everyday electricity customers and communities near power plants came out ahead; coal mining companies and coal-burning utilities came out behind.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Power plant neighbors, not coal operators

for.name: Ed Whitfield
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Power
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, steered it through subcommittee and committee, and managed its floor consideration.

for.name: 219 of 231 House Republicans
for.role: House Republican conference on final passage
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage, 219-3, supplying nearly all of the 229 votes.

for.name: 10 of 199 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage over their party's opposition.

against.name: 180 of 199 House Democrats
against.role: House Democratic conference on final passage
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage, and all but 3 voted for the motion to recommit protecting consumer-saving efficiency rules.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: The administration opposed the bill, which would have erased EPA power plant rules his EPA had proposed, and his advisers were reported to recommend a veto had it reached his desk.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a Senate floor vote; it sat on the Senate calendar from May 2014 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split almost entirely by party: 219 of 231 Republicans yes against 10 of 199 Democrats yes, and the consumer-protection motion to recommit drew 184 Democratic yes votes and zero Republican yes votes.

industries.note: The bill would have made a carbon standard for new coal plants impossible and wiped out proposed rules, protecting demand for coal. The industry's gain would come at the cost of continued greenhouse gas emissions and the pollution limits the public would otherwise get.

They would be freed from carbon standards for new plants and would need a new act of Congress before any rule reached their existing or upgraded plants. Their avoided compliance costs are the public's lost emissions reductions.

The bill bars using demonstration project results to set standards, undercutting the technology pathway the EPA's proposed rule relied on. Their interest in deploying carbon capture runs alongside the public's interest in cutting emissions.

Requiring separate coal and gas categories would let a standard for new gas plants rest on technology hundreds of existing gas units already achieve, so new gas rules could go forward. But the bill would also block limits on existing gas plants until Congress acted.
